newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Animals, nature and money top citizens' worry list.
newsitem.headline: Animals, nature and money top citizens' worry list.

text.p: Outrage about animal welfare, damage to the environment and money problems were among the subjects which most irritated Europeans in the past year and had them taking their miseries to the European Parliament.

More than 1,000 petitions dropped into parliament's petitions committee postbag between March 1996 and March 1997, many with the signatures of more than 10,000 disgruntled citizens, according to a report to be presented to Euro-MPs on Monday by British Conservative Roy Perry.

As in the past, petitions with the largest number of supporting signatures concerned animal welfare, with more than four million people putting their names to a protest about experiments on animals by the cosmetics industry.
In 1994 well over three million European Union citizens urged the EU assembly to act against cruelty to horses transported vast distances across the EU for slaughter.

Last month, a further 50,000 people pleaded with the parliament to pressure the British and Irish governments to lift their quarantine rules on domestic pets. Officials say there is a regular stream of complaints about the issue.
There is not always a lot that parliament can do to answer the appeals.

This is partly because it only has the power to deal with allegations of maladministration by EU institutions -- such as its executive Commission, the Council of Ministers and parliament itself -- partly because EU governments are reluctant to cooperate in providing information, Perry's report says.

Nevertheless, it got positive results for a number of petitioners last year, in some cases leading to the European Commission initiating infringement proceedings against national governments for failing to apply EU law.
In one case, a Greek petitioner complained about air pollution from schemes run by the Greek Electricity Board and partly financed by the EU's Regional Development Fund.
Commission action forced the Athens government to start clean-up measures.

In another case, the Commission started proceedings against The Hague after a Spanish pensioner living in the Netherlands protested that the Dutch authorities paid full pension benefits to all non-resident pensioners except the Spanish, who had 20 percent taken off in tax.
It remains to be seen what will happen to last month's 50,000-signature plea for an end to quarantine for pets.

In response to action by the petitions committee on a similar, earlier plea, the Commission said last year that rabies was likely to disappear from the EU "in the not too distant future", that alternatives to quarantine were already in place for traded animals, and that it would propose alternatives for domestic pets "at an appropriate time".

In fact, the Commission has such a proposal already prepared but it has not been a high priority and was, until the change of government in Britain last month, seen as something Euro-sceptic British Conservatives would seize on to claim that Brussels was letting rabies into the country, an EU official told Reuters.
Britain's junior farm minister Jeff Hooker said last week he would look into the problem, but an Irish official in Brussels said Dublin had no plans to change policy.
